A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8583. Your Credit History From Home Can Get You a U.S. Card – No Deposit Needed

Good credit in your home country can still count in the U.S. If home is the United Kingdom or Canada, Chase can use your credit history there. If you’ve held a card from American Express itself abroad for at least three months, Amex can use that account. Check both before you settle for a card that needs a deposit.

A U.S. credit file starts empty, however long your record abroad. So a newcomer with years of on-time payments looks like a first-time borrower, the kind who usually starts on a secured card, backed by a cash deposit.

Chase can use the credit history you built in the U.K. or Canada, through Nova Credit, a company that converts a foreign credit report into a U.S.-style report and score. For now, Chase does this only on the Freedom Unlimited and the Freedom Flex.

American Express uses a different record, the Amex card you hold in another country. If Amex itself issued that card, not a partner bank, you’re its main cardholder, and you’ve had it at least three months, Amex may base its decision on that account’s history. Keep it open and in good standing until you apply, or apply within three months of closing it. You can apply for one U.S. card this way, and for more once you’ve built U.S. credit.

On Chase’s application, check the box asking Chase to consider your international credit history, then follow any instructions Chase sends for your report. For Amex, pick the U.S. American Express card you want, click the Already a Card Member link on its application, and enter your current account number, U.S. home address, and U.S. phone number. Amex takes passport details if you don’t have a Social Security number yet.

Say a nurse moves from Canada with a Social Security number, a U.S. address, and eight years of on-time payments on her Canadian report. Checking the box on a Freedom Unlimited application can get her a regular card, no deposit needed. A colleague with the same record who skips the box spends her first year on a secured card.

Newcomers who fit neither route can open a Chase checking or savings account with at least $250, then apply for the Freedom Rise, a Chase card for people new to credit. Chase says that balance improves your approval odds, and a secured card stays your backup.

#8580. Upgrading To A Home You Don’t Need: A Three-Year Review

Toward the end of 2023, we upgraded to a larger finished home we didn't need. Three years later, I want to share whether it was worth it, so you can make a better decision if you're tempted to do the same.

More than any other material item money can buy, a home is the most desirable. The average person spends over 14 hours a day at home, so there's also probably no investment we use more. Sure, we have to wear clothes in public, but we swap them out every day. And last I checked, my t-shirts and shoes don't appreciate in value.

Fine watches and jewelry are nice and can appreciate too. But we don't wear them every day, and we definitely don't live inside them. So hands down, a home is the best combination of enjoying your money while also potentially making a positive return.

Upgrading to a home you don't need is a slightly different animal.

If you upgrade into something other people find undesirable or unnecessary, your home probably won't give you a positive return you're hoping for. But if you upgrade in the “frenzy zone” price range, the one buyers fight over in your market, you'll almost always have strong demand when it's your turn to sell.

My wife and I talked about this on our podcast, and we've concluded the purchase was worth it.

It took a tremendous amount of convincing to get her to agree to move. She finally acquiesced after I promised this would be our last house ever, assuming we stay in San Francisco. That promise was the main thing that got her over the line.

Our children have enjoyed the extra space tremendously. They play in the enclosed front yard every day, and we don't have to worry about them getting hit by a car or snatched by a stranger. The neighborhood is quiet and safe, although there's now a lot of remodeling going on.

I've also noticed our boy needs to run around more than our daughter, which seems typical. Once he's burned off the energy, it's easier to get him to focus on homework.

If you have a boy, or any extremely active child, a home on a large, usable lot can be beneficial for childhood development. That's something we didn't fully appreciate before buying.

There's also peace in knowing we'll never move again. For 20 years, from 2003 to 2023, I was addicted to real estate and constantly climbing the property ladder. Now that we've reached the top rung we can afford, I feel settled in a way I didn't expect. No more wanting feels amazing!

If you're focused on decumulation, or at least on spending more of the hard-earned money and risky investments that have paid off, it feels good to turn that money into something you actually enjoy.

A nicer home checks the box of being something we use every single day, which is more than I can say for most things I've spent on.

From a purely financial standpoint, the toughest part of upgrading to a home you don't need is thinking about how much more you could have made had you invested elsewhere, usually in stocks.

The S&P 500 is up over 80% since we sold stocks and Treasury bonds to buy our home. The opportunity cost of not making more elsewhere must be weighed against the utility you derived from your home.

It could always be worse, though. I talked to one dad who sold his Salesforce (CRM) stock in 2009 to buy his home. Had he held on, the stock would be up about 10X. I talked to another dad, currently thinking about upgrading, who worked at Tesla and sold shares in 2015 to buy his place. That stock is up more than 20X since.

Both of their properties are also up since purchase. But their old stock positions are up dramatically more.

All in, I'm sure I've left over $1 million on the table by buying our house, net of how much the house has appreciated. The opportunity cost could have been worse, but luckily the San Francisco housing market is strong thanks to AI. It's boom loop time.

I'm not sure we could buy our house today if it came on the market. In 24 years of searching for property in San Francisco, I've never seen a lot this size at this price point. So maybe the market is adjusting higher than I think, especially as the west side of San Francisco gets more popular.

The general recommendation is to set aside 1% of your home's value each year for maintenance. It's a decent rule of thumb, especially if you own a condo with a homeowners association, which I also do.

But after three years in the house, here's what we've actually spent:

That's roughly $4,700 over three years, or about $1,567 a year for pure maintenance. Practically nothing, and far below the 1% rule of thumb.

The low cost isn't entirely luck. We were thorough during the three-month escrow and had the sellers fix as much as possible before closing. The house had also been gut remodeled and fully landscaped right before our purchase, so we bought near the top of its maintenance cycle, not the bottom.

Run through this checklist before you fall in love and experience buyer’s remorse:

1) Make sure your spouse is genuinely on board. Not “fine, whatever” on board. Actually on board and extremely excited. A reluctant partner turns a great house into a recurring argument. Make a promise you can keep, like I did, and mean it.

2) Run the 30/30/3-5 rule. Have at least 30% of the purchase price saved (20% down, 10% buffer), keep the monthly payment under 30% of your gross income, and limit the home price to no more than 3 to 5 times your annual gross income. Break this rule and you invite stress.

3) Buy just above the frenzy zone. Pick a home and neighborhood that buyers fight over, then look for a price point about 10% higher. The frenzy zone is where most people bid, which means bidding wars that can leave you with tremendous buyer’s remorse if you win. Just above it, there’s less competition and better deals.

3) Stress test your cash flow. Model the new mortgage, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, then assume one income disappears for six months. If the math gives you a panic attack, you’re stretching too far. I went through a six-month period of living paycheck to paycheck which recreated the stress I felt in banking almost every day.

4) Decide mortgage vs. cash with your opportunity cost in mind. Before you sell investments, ask what that money would likely earn if you left it alone, because that’s the cost you’ll feel most. Paying cash removes the monthly payment but concentrates your money in one illiquid asset. A mortgage keeps more invested but costs you fees, paperwork, and a lien.

If you can afford to pay cash and the home is worth 30% or less of your net worth after purchase, the cash route makes sense with interest rates this high. You can often get a better deal, or win the bid, by closing quickly with cash.

5) Hire an inspector and use a long escrow. This is where you create leverage. Find every defect and push the seller to fix as much as possible before closing. Our low maintenance bill is a direct result of being relentless during escrow.

6) Match the home to your family’s actual life. Active kids need a lot to run around on. Aging parents with bad hips prefer a single-story or a guest suite. Buy for how you’ll really live now and in the future, not for the staged photos, and not to impress people who aren’t paying your property tax bill.

In conclusion, we would happily buy this home again. The experience has worked out, but of course, it could easily have not. I cannot get these three years back, but I can appreciate how this house has provided a nicer life for my wife and children.

The one thing I might change is taking out a mortgage so I wouldn't have had to sell so much stock. But a mortgage would have cost about $10,000 in fees upfront, plus more work, plus the bank holding a lien. So maybe not.

Money is meant to be spent and enjoyed while we're still alive. So if you want to upgrade your home, go right ahead. Just follow the 30/30/3-5 rule so you don't put yourself in financial jeopardy and end up too stressed to enjoy the place.

Readers, have you ever upgraded to a home you didn't need? Was it worth it, or do you wish you'd kept the money invested? And if you're on the fence right now, what's holding you back?

Upgrading our home concentrated a big chunk of our net worth in one illiquid asset on one street in one city. Great for the kids. Not great for diversification.

If you want more real estate exposure without selling stocks, fixing fence planks, or paying a plumber at 10pm, take a look at Fundrise. AI may be the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs a physical home. Hyperscalers are pouring hundreds of billions a year into data centers, and power and permitting have become the binding constraint. Real estate is where that constraint gets solved.

My wife and I recorded a podcast episode looking back on our first three years in the house as well, including whether she’s forgiven me for convincing her to move. It's also a great discussion about life after FIRE, parenthood, and tackling growing desires. Listen on Apple or Spotify.

We recently upgraded our home into my “stretch” zone. We lived in our previous home for 13 years with the intent on keeping it as a rental, +3x the value and low 30 year mortgage

When our new house came up in January this year there was a bidding war and we won. I’m confident it could have gone higher but the seller only wanted to market it for 5 days. We put down 31.5% on the purchase with a 7 year I/O at 5.25%.

I’ve felt a lot of stress when I think of the big picture because I’m somewhat risk adverse. We kept our house with a great tenant for two years that exceeded my rent expectations.

When I get overwhelmed, I step back and take a hot tub (private gate into association pool/hot tub) and look around and realize I’ve upgraded my family to one of the nicest best run beach cities in SoCal. They aren’t making more land, the house brings immense joy to me and my family. We are off the busy street we lived in before and it’s so much more peaceful, safer.

I’ve reached deep into AI to help when I get stressed and it validates the purchase math, my investment thesis, and my belief in the area we invested.

While my business has been down, 100% commission, in the end of the day I realize much of my stress is my mind playing tricks one me by playing out worst case scenarios. The psychology of making life changing big moves is really something else. In a few years, I’ll be more comfortable as I grow into our new reality. Buffet always talks about the psychology of investing and it’s a real doozy.

Yes indeed. The stress of making big investment decisions can really get to you.

In three years, your home should feel much more affordable. Hope you can enjoy it as much as possible.

Better than losing / giving up all your gains in tech stocks this year!

Interesting perspective! Upgrading to a bigger home can be exciting, but the additional costs and long-term financial commitment are important to consider. I think choosing a home based on actual needs and financial comfort is often better than upgrading just for extra space. Thanks for sharing your thoughts!

Sam, Would you watch or update the “30% of your net worth” home purchase rule to reflect home value as it appreciates? Suppose your purchase fits well within that rule at first, but doubles (hey, it could happen) in only a couple years. Now you have significant equity but also very high taxes, insurance, and perhaps even higher maintenance costs. How does that square?

If the home itself surges in value much faster than your overall net worth growth, then it’s just a reason to feel great about your purchase. There’s no need to sell it and buy a new house to get it down to 30% or lower. Enjoy the great purchase and the good times.

The extra cost should be affordable if you bought anywhere near the other two variables.

Regarding the 30/30/3-5 rules, it seems that it’s dependent on income. In other words, a 100K income on 500K home and small down payment vs 500K income with large down payment on 2.5M home looks a lot different. If coming in with a large down payment, that would seemingly impact the 3-5Xs income rule quite a bit vs 3-5Xs the entire purchase price?

Scenarios: 500K income 2.65M purchase price 1.275M down payment 1.375M mortgage

It’s a general guideline to hit within the ranges of the three variables.

The down payment variable is more powerful, where if you put a larger down payment down, you can do a higher multiple of income.

The down payment is more certain, but the income variable can change at any moment.

Figured. Ok, looking to upgrade to a home we don’t need that has quite a few scarcity features that aren’t easy to replicate, so likely a now or never scenario.

It is surprising how fast three years have passed by. We bought a house four years ago with cash, and I am nodding my head in agreement with each of your points. If I had kept the home purchase money invested in Apple, that stock’s value would have doubled. I am reminded of Charlie Munger’s quote, “The first rule of compounding: Never interrupt it unnecessarily.”

Also, the home purchase price pushed up against your “30% or less of net worth” rule.

Neither of these issues have created financial stress in our lives, and we own a very nice house. And, if this home turns into our “forever home” I will also have a “forever job” of fixing things. LOL

That’s great things have worked out. And mainly it’s probably because you spent reasonably, and within my guidelines.

Getting to the point of buying too much house, over five times you’re gross income, and hoping your job will continue to be there and your income will continue to grow is very risky proposition in this market.

What a fun recap and glad to hear it’s worked out well for your family. Any relocation, even if it’s just from one street to the next around the corner, is a big commitment of time, energy, and often higher cost. Any major change is always a risk so that’s great it was worth it for you. There’s also something incredibly priceless about feeling settled and not having to move again. Enjoy your home!

#8579. Six Long Walks Across Australia in 2026

A number of long-distance solo walks have been taking place across Australia this year. Some started in 2026, others ended this year. The walkers have all taken different routes. Some are pulling trailers, others wheelbarrows, and one man is doing it dressed in a leopard-print onesie.

Musician Britt Franzmann, known as Birdgirl, spent much of 2026 walking 3,125km from Perth to Melbourne. She started in May, camped along the route, and carried her equipment in a cart. Speaking to SuzieScribbles, she said she has been obsessed with the idea of crossing the country on foot since reading Robyn Davidson’s book, Tracks. She wanted to see what it was like to be in the remote areas of Australia and do something far outside her comfort zone. From the start, she has been very clear about the rules for her expedition: no support vehicles and no shortcuts.

The logistics became one of the defining features of the walk, mainly because Franzmann was pushing her belongings rather than carrying a backpack. Even though this meant she could take more through remote backcountry areas, including (most importantly) her guitar, it also meant that terrain, heat, and the condition of the cart became constant considerations. More than once, the cart fell apart and needed repairs so that she could continue.

The isolation was one of the hardest parts. For huge sections, she had almost no human contact. Franzmann describes herself as an introvert, but she relishes meeting people on the road and having a chat. A huge boost came in mid-June when her dad joined her for a few days. At the same time, it made the loneliness feel more severe when he left.

Along the way, she often focused on reaching the next big town. Two-thirds of the way through, she decided not to do that. She also stopped turning her trek into social media content. After walking for just over four months, Franzmann made it to Melbourne and finished by performing a homecoming concert at the Northcote Social Club.

Mark Gresser completed his 6,023km walk across Australia in 331 days. He started hiking from Steep Point in Western Australia to Cape Byron in New South Wales in July 2025 and reached his endpoint in June 2026. Of the 331 days, 223 were spent walking. His route went via Lambert’s Centre, Australia’s geographical midpoint, and he covered around 35km a day, walking up to eight or nine hours daily. With temperatures reaching 50°C at times, he followed the weather rather than a particular schedule.

Unlike several other journeys in this roundup, Gresser’s expedition was genuinely solo and self-supported. He had no vehicle support, and his route took him through some of the remotest parts of the country, with limited water sources. His solution to the huge distances between settlements was to pull a 1.9m wheeled cart that carried up to 200kg of food, water, clothing, and equipment. Before setting out, he dehydrated hundreds of meals and posted them to resupply points along the route.

He had to modify the route and take a more southerly path when his cart could not make it over the sand dunes of the Simpson Desert. Yet he could not avoid sand entirely. In the Strzelecki Desert, it took him 18 days to cover 463 km, including 120km over dunes. Many were too steep to pull the cart over, forcing him to repeatedly unpack it and shuttle his load in stages.

A view from the tent. Photo: Mark Gresser

Kentaro Jin, who dubs himself the Strange Catman, started his journey in November 2023. Armed with a wheelbarrow of supplies and sporting a leopard-print onesie, he set out from Carnarvon, Western Australia, and started walking toward the Sydney Opera House. Two-and-a-half years and 6,400km later, he made it to Sydney.

He started the journey after breaking up with his girlfriend in Japan. Speaking to We Are Explorers, he said he felt that his “reason for living crumbled in an instant” and so decided to do something he had thought of when he was a student — a long-distance journey.

In 2024, when he had passed 1,000km, Jin told ABC that he was walking for 10 hours every day and sleeping in a tent beside the road during the long stretches between towns. In civilization, he often stayed with locals, making the most of any hospitality offered. One reason his walk took years to complete was that he stopped periodically to rest and work.

The wheelbarrow may seem like an unusual choice, but it was not a gimmick. He was just used to using one. “I felt a sense of destiny with the wheelbarrow. I worked in construction for six years, and the wheelbarrow was a familiar tool,” he commented.

He finally reached the Sydney Opera House on March 14, 2026, but decided to extend the journey. Now he is cycling along Australia’s east coast, pulling the wheelbarrow behind him, and still in his cat-man outfit.

Simon Harvey, also known as Captain Australia, completed his Big Lap of Australia in April of this year. He began from Brisbane in July 2023 and eventually returned to King George Square in his home city after walking over 15,000km around mainland Australia.

He originally estimated that he would walk 30–35km per day, at least six days a week. That meant around 18 months of walking. In reality, the journey stretched across almost three years due to the number of rest periods he needed and the practicalities of life on the road.

Harvey was never going to do this as an unsupported walk, and relied heavily on the network of people he met along the way. Nor was he always solo. On many occasions, he was joined by his wife, friends, and locals he met along the way.  After finishing the walk, he told The Kids’ Cancer Project that he had been given “fresh pairs of boots, hot meals, and countless conversations by people encountered on the road.”

‘Captain Australia.’ Photo: Peri Strathearn

Walking has always been part of Harvey’s life. When he was just 15, he left home and walked from Brisbane to Sydney to live with his grandmother. Years later, having watched his business fall apart during COVID and then battling cancer, he decided it was time to start walking again. “The walk was my vehicle for healing,” he explained.

One Step Max, who has no other public name, is taking a very different approach from everyone else walking across Australia. His journey has no fixed route, no declared finish line, and by his own account, deliberately no plan.

“When I first started this journey, the first rule I made was to make no plans,” he told the Junee Independent. “That way, I can never be disappointed because I never know what’s going to turn up. So, if I need to spend time with somebody, I’ve got time up my sleeve.”

He set off in October 2025 and walked from Albury to Adelaide for two months along the Murray River. He then took a break to avoid the summer heat before starting to walk again.

“I started on the NSW-Queensland border,” Max told the Junee Bulletin. “I went from Goondiwindi to Moree, Bingara, Narrabri and Tamworth, then from Coonabarabran to Forbes, Condobolin, Lake Cargelligo, West Wyalong, back to Forbes, back to West Wyalong, and then Temora.” Now he is walking through Junee.

Max is also the second person in this roundup who decided a wheelbarrow was the best option for toting his kit and supplies. As the warmer seasons approached, he removed 30kg of winter clothing and gear from his wheelbarrow to pare down his load.

The wheelbarrow setup. Photo: One Step Max

His journey is part of a much larger campaign to walk 700,000km, representing the more than 700,000 people estimated to die by suicide globally each year. That would mean walking the equivalent of 18 circuits of the Earth’s equator. According to the Junee Independent, “The suicide awareness advocate has walked almost 155,000 kilometers so far and is now on his fourth lap of the Earth.”

Steve Roberts began his 4,200km walk across Australia on September 14. At first, he considered starting on the east coast at Cape Byron, but as he has no personal connection to that area, he decided to switch the starting point to Coonamble, the town where he was born. His planned route takes him west through Bourke and Broken Hill before crossing the Nullarbor to Perth.

By the end of September, he had walked 350km and reached Bourke. As with the other walkers, meeting locals is an important part of the journey. He regularly chats to people along the route, and has found himself accepting water top-ups, hot showers, and home-cooked meals.

On reaching Bourke, he rested for a few days. The expedition is not about setting speed records. Robert’s father died at the age of 50 — the age he is now. This walk is to prove “that turning 50 isn’t the end of the story.” Roberts has given himself more than 140 days for the 4,200km route, an average of around 30km per day, though this fluctuates depending on the terrain, weather, and how he is feeling on the day. He is now making his way toward Broken Hill.

Unlike other expeditions, this is not an unsupported hike. Apart from many pre-positioned caches of food and water, his family is accompanying him in a support van.

At the end of November, he will take a 10-day break with his family, then resume from where he left off. Regardless of the style of his journey, he has been very clear about one thing — he will walk every one of the 4,200km on foot.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8578. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:30 pm

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

Because stocks tend to have inflation protection built in over the long run (both share prices and dividends rise with the currency numbers over time, plus you get any premium created by earnings growth)

Okay but with all that aside: I think I’ll always stay all-stock. Because volatility is only a problem for people who worry about fluctuating prices – the odds are still in your favor with an all-stock portfolio even when you are getting old.

Also note that if you own a house with no mortgage, that’s pretty big form of inflation-adjusted bond right there because it kicks out the equivalent of a rent payment that never goes up. And the principal portion (the value of your home) also keeps up with inflation which you can always cash out in the future if you change your mind or need to pay for long-term care or leave a big estate.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

Early in my career as a self-employed contractor, I would call up my buddy regularly to worry aloud how would I ever have enough work to feed my growing family.

This fear was valid. If I wanted them to eat, I had to buy food. If I wanted to buy food I needed money. To get money I needed paid work. To get paid work I had to sell jobs.

My buddy eventually reminded me that in between calling him up to worry aloud about not having enough work, I would also call him up regularly to beg him to help me with all the work I suddenly had lined up and now I wasn’t sure how I would get it all done!

Until he put it to me that way, I was too caught up in the moment to realize what I had been doing.

So, which is it? Are we afraid of not having enough? Or are we afraid of having too much?

Let’s not be afraid of either one. Either way, we are adaptable, capable and full of badassity!

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:24 pm

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

#8576. Superniño Weather Threatens Aconcagua Season

The Aconcagua climbing season is approaching, but the threat of unstable conditions linked to this year’s superniño is causing headaches for expedition operators, guides, climbers, and rescue teams.

Temperatures on the surface of the Pacific Ocean are so high that the weather phenomenon usually known as El Niño (the boy) has become a superniño for 2026. Warm, wet air from the ocean can result in massive precipitation inland, and for Aconcagua — South America’s highest peak — that means lots of snow.

A graphic illustrating increasing temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.

Argentina’s meteorological service forecasts a colder, more humid spring than usual, both in coastal areas and in Patagonia, the location of Aconcagua. Authorities in Argentina’s mountain province of Mendoza are issuing weather alerts that warn of flooding and intense snow. Several mountain passes are closed and neighboring Chile is also enduring intense rain and snowfall. The webcams at Portillo ski resort, 27km from Aconcagua, show winter-like images.

The effects of the superniño may unfold over several months. It will surely change conditions in mountain areas by the time the Aconcagua season starts in November for trekking groups, and on December 1 for climbing expeditions. Local guiding companies fear that snow-covered trails and flooded rivers may isolate lower camps. Further up the mountain, climbers might have to progress on icy ramps instead of scree slopes, and deal with significant avalanche risk.

Given the circumstances, park authorities will wait before announcing when the season will begin. Local media suggest either December 5 or December 15 as tentative opening dates.

“The [super] niño will reach its maximum intensity in December, when the temperature of the Central Pacific Ocean will be +2.7°C higher than normal,” meteorologists told La Gaceta.

#8574. Trekking and Packrafting 700Km Across Northern Siberia

Two Russian explorers have completed a journey of about 700km across the remote Putorana Plateau in northern Siberia. During their expedition, they encountered drought conditions, wildfires, and a brazen bear that raided their food supplies.

Danil Barashkov and Sergey Malykh set off in early July. They flew to the small town of Svetlogorsk in northern Siberia, before taking a motorboat up the Kureika River system toward Lake Dupkun. On July 7, they started on foot across the Putorana Plateau from a nearby scientific research base.

A mountainous region between 67°N and 70°N in the Arctic Circle, the plateau is the size of Great Britain. Featuring some 25,000 lakes, it is the second-largest store of fresh water in Russia after Lake Baikal. The men set out with 40kg packs and entered the plateau’s remote eastern section, expecting to use packrafts for most of their journey. Instead, they found drought conditions, with water levels too low to paddle, and even drinking water in short supply.

“There was almost no rain all of June. So we ended up like this: ‘I’m standing on the pavement, wearing skis.’ We arrived with our packrafts, and there was no water,” Malykh told Russian news site NGS24.RU. Though water was scarce, the mosquitoes remained. “I’ve never seen anything like this before: you lift the lid of the pot, and there’s a layer of mosquitoes floating around. Yeah, we definitely had no problem with protein.”

The pair found very dry conditions early in their trip. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Their original plan was to cross the plateau and continue to the settlement of Khatanga in northern Siberia. However, the exceptionally dry conditions forced a change of plan. Instead, they crossed toward the upper basin of the Kotuy River, 300km of hiking that sometimes required shuttles to move their gear. They covered only 15km per day and realized that their trip would run longer than their initial six-week plan. But this slog paid off; from the Kotuy, they could finally use their packrafts.

Barashkov and Malykh had a few scary bear encounters. In one instance, they almost walked into a sleeping bear, and in another, a curious bear only retreated from their campsite after coming as close as 15 meters — and after ignoring their shouts and a shot from a flare gun.

A bear that didn’t come too close. Photo: Danil Barashkov

However, the worst instance came after they cached some food. A bear had found the supplies and was still eating them when they returned. With hundreds of kilometers still to travel, Barashkov and Malykh couldn’t afford to lose everything. They collected their bear deterrents and managed to briefly scare the bear away before hurriedly packing what remained of their food into their backpacks and escaping downwind.

Over the next three weeks, they used packrafts to travel 400km and their luck improved. They found plentiful berries and caught fish in the river to supplement their remaining food.

Their arrival at Chirinda in the second half of August marked the end of their expedition after around 60 days. Yet forest fires forced the pair to remain in the village for another 10 days. Wildfires swept through the surrounding tundra forests and smothered the area in smoke, grounding flights.

Wildfire smoke near the village of Chirinda. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8573. Russian Team Moving Up on Everest

The only team currently on Everest has set off across an untouched Khumbu Icefall. There are no ladders or ropes at this time of year, and everything ahead of them is uncertain.

Earlier this week, the Russian team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina acclimatized toward the Nuptse shoulder, to the right of the Khumbu Icefall. Heavy snow slowed them, eventually forcing them to stop for the night at 5,650m.

Nuptse in the sun, with the Khumbu Glacier at the base and Everest’s West Shoulder on the left. Photo: Russian Everest Expedition 2026

Returning to their quarters in Lobuche, the team focused on rest and pondered their options. “We are considering two alternatives: either going up across the Khumbu Icefall or trying the West Ridge via the Lho La, the mountain pass to the left of the Khumbu Glacier that leads to Everest’s west ridge,” they said. Jost Kobusch has attempted the West Ride/Lho La route several times in winter.

The Russians have now chosen the first option. “We’re heading up, attempting to get through the Khumbu Icefall,” Vasilief told Mountainclub. “We’ll see how things go from there.”

The team plans to spend six days on the mountain and has not confirmed whether they will attempt the summit or complete another partial trip.

#8571. Weekend Warm-Up: Sending Ivindo Falls

Gabon Uncharted: Sending Ivindo Falls follows a crew of young kayakers, as they attempt to paddle 150km down the Ivindo River’s many rapids, gorges, and waterfalls.

The four kayakers are what the film’s narrator calls the “top of the crop.” After taking a moment to admire this charming malaphor (I think our narrator has combined “cream of the crop” and “top of the class”) we meet the Send team. Leader Adrian Mattern of Germany spent years planning their trip to Gabon, bringing with him the talkative Dane Jackson, patient Kalob Grady, and Bren Orton. Orton signed on with the shiny-faced, inevitably short-lived optimism of a youngster in 1914 headed for the front, sure of being home by Christmas.

“Apparently,” the narrator notes, “no one told him what he was getting into on this trip.”

Once on the ground, they load up their supplies and set out on a long stretch of flat water. Struggling along behind, we meet the film crew, an interesting behind-the-scenes look at the process of filming a professional, well-funded adventure documentary. Filmmaker Olaf Obsommer, photographer David Sodomka, and narrator David Arnaud do everything the Send team does, backward and in heels. Or, no — I’m thinking of Ginger Rogers.

Obsommer was part of the first team to scout the river by kayak in 2007. They portaged past most of the rapids for safety. Nowadays, better kayaks and the ability to scout ahead by drone will, hopefully, let them complete what he started.

At the first of four whitewater sections, Kongou, they settle in to take the rocky labyrinth piece by piece. If they take the wrong branch, they’ll be heading over a 25m waterfall.

Adrian is entranced by Kongou Falls, and only when the team delicately sit him down and explain that he would very likely drown, which would be awkward, does he agree to move on. Photo: Screenshot

They work their way down the river looking for rapids that will not kill them immediately. On the way, they get advice from Juste Parfait Zangonga, a local expert, on how to not be killed by elephants, gorillas, crocodiles, vipers, or hippos.

The next rapids, Mingouli, are less maze, more rollercoaster. The Send team can finally start living up to their name. Between first descents, they paddle past a family of elephants and get devoured by insects.

First descent down a tricky section of Mingouli. Photo: Screenshot

Kouata Mango, section three, is where Mattern finally gets to send a massive waterfall. The team agrees that this one is less likely to kill him badly, and over the side he goes.

Tsengue Lelendi, the final set of rapids, rounds out the trip. The laconic Kaleb takes a look at one particularly rough section and tells our narrator that the rapid is unrunnable. The rest of the team spends a long time debating it, anyway. Lo and behold, he’s right. After scouting with drones, mapping every angle, and discussing the route at length, they agree to skip a section of the rapid. The chain will still have just a few missing links left.

“A part of this river will remain untouched,” Arnaud concludes, “as it should, probably.”
