#8448. Andrew Skurka’s 2027 Pacific Crest Trail Backpacking Gear List

I first hiked the Pacific Crest Trail in 2006, and I went through the High Sierra in late June, early July. I was wearing running shorts, like short running shorts, a T-shirt, a visor. I had like a 40-liter backpack.

I had no way to protect myself from bugs, no way to protect myself from sun. I’ve learned a lot in the intervening years. I am fortunate enough to backpack in the High Sierra basically every year.

You can’t go wrong with the High Sierra. Bang for your buck, it’s like one of the greatest places in the world. You have phenomenal scenery, wonderful bluebird skies for the most part during the summer, majestic crystal-clear lakes, some biting insects, but it’s like a short-lived season, blissful off-trail travel, a lot to love.

If you’re planning on hiking the Pacific Crest Trail in 2027, this gear list should really help you out. It will also be relevant towards any of the other trips that you might do in the High Sierra. If you’re going to do, say, a section on the John Muir Trail, if you’re going to do the Sierra High Route, Yosemite High Route, Kings Canyon High Basin Route, and if you’re just going to do a weekend out of Fallen Leaf Meadows or out of Lodgepole or out of, say, Piute Pass.

I would make some slight adjustments to this gear list based on exactly what month I’d be up there. So I’m going to give you a kit that works between the months of like June and September. I also would make a few tweaks if I was a female instead of a male, and I would also make a few tweaks if I had a last-minute forecast that was notably warmer and drier or cooler and wetter than the average.

Today, we’re going to cover the entire kit, starting with what I would wear, and then we’ll go to inside my backpack. We’ll talk about my sleep system, shelter, food storage, and my cook system.

Hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. I’m a former thru-hiker and was the first person to do the Sea-to-Sea Route, the Great Western Loop, and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition. I’ve also, in the Sierra, hiked the John Muir Trail at least once. The Sierra High Route, I put together the Yosemite High Route and the Kings Canyon High Basin Route.

I guide trips there every single year. Typically, we’re there during late July and August. This is part of a weekly video series that I do with The Trek.

We drop a new video every Monday at noon Mountain Time. One announcement before we get started. We’re doing a live event with Backpacker Radio on December 5th, Saturday, at Skylark Lounge in Denver.

If you’re a resident of the Denver metro area, you can get tickets here.

To start, let’s talk about the go-suit. The go-suit is defined as the things that I’m going to be wearing or carrying directly on my body all day long. It doesn’t matter what the conditions are.

Let me just start with the shirt. I’m going to be wearing a long-sleeve hoodie, and I’m going to be wearing a ball cap.

This hoodie has been permethrin-treated, so it’ll keep the biting insects, particularly the mosquitoes, off of me during peak season, which in the Sierra, usually peak mosquito season, it’ll start maybe like middle of June and it’s starting to wind down after about mid-July. Usually by August 1st, there are almost no mosquitoes in the Sierra.

The timing and the mosquito season definitely varies, though, with the winter snowpack, so whenever you’re watching this, make sure to get an update on what the winter has been and what sort of the forecast is for when the mosquitoes will hatch and how bad they might be.

If I was starting the Pacific Crest Trail in Mexico, you basically would not have changed your shirt. You would want almost an identical shirt for that section where you’re dealing with a lot of sun exposure, and also at that time of the year, like in April, you’re gonna be dealing with some cooler temperatures, so you would actually appreciate the warmth of a long sleeve.

It would not need to be permethrin-treated because you don’t have a biting insect issue in that part of the trail, but you would appreciate having a long sleeve for the sun protection.

The hood also gives you sun protection, and also at that time of the year, you might be starting in March or April, you might want a little bit of warmth that the long sleeve and that the hood provides.

For bottoms, okay, so I have on a pair of shorts, and shorts, they’re just better than pants. Better range of motion, better ventilation, and if I can get away with shorts, I’m gonna wear shorts.

I do, though, always carry with me a pair of pants, and the pants, there are like a couple of different scenarios here. So if I was hiking the Pacific Crest Trail, absolutely, I’d be trying to hike as many miles as I could in shorts, but I still would bring pants because there are times where I need that extra sun protection, or if I’m traveling or if I’m hiking, if I’m on the trail during bug season, then you definitely would want the biting resistance of a full pair of pants.

The last thing to consider would be if you are in the High Sierra early in the season when there’s still snow lingering on the ground. Again, you’re going to need pants because the snow is super reflective, and you’ll get scorched if you just are wearing shorts.

I remember, you hear about how intense the sun is in the West, but if you’re not from here, you might not have ever experienced it.

The first weekend I ever was in Colorado, this was back in 2003, I went backpacking up at the Indian Peaks. Everyone had told me, yeah, you know, the sun is a lot more intense here than it was in North Carolina where I was going to school at the time, and I didn’t believe them, so I went out in my normal Appalachian Trail outfit of short shorts and a T-shirt.

And when I got back into the office on Monday morning, I realized that the back of my hamstrings actually were blistered because I had gotten sunburned so badly on my hamstrings, remarkably.

So the sun out here is real. You’re going to want a pair of pants, even if you want to do the bulk of your miles in shorts.

“Creek crossings in the High Sierra warrant your attention. The hazard is caused by a unique set of circumstances: Significant wintertime snowfall, Arrival of hot and sunny weather in late-spring, Steep gradients, Few bridges, Recreational use miles downstream of headwaters, and, Non-porous granite substrate.” (Skurka)

Another item that’s included in my go-suit would be a pair of sungloves. This is one of those items that I added in the last 10 years, after I did the bulk of my thru-hikes, and I remember wearing, using them for the first time and just thinking like, oh wow, where have you been my entire life?

They’re great for added sun protection. They provide some abrasion resistance against my trekking poles. If you’re doing any off-trail travel, you can grab onto sharp rocks or use veggie belays without risk of cutting up your hands.

These sungloves that I have, this is actually a pair of deerskin gloves made by Milwaukee that I bought at my local Home Depot, because I find them to be, they’re less expensive, but more importantly, a lot more durable than sunglove-specific products like these Glacier Gloves.

But these are really nice. They breathe better, they’re lighter, they’re just more comfortable to wear, but they don’t last that long. Maybe give them like a month before you kind of burn through the faux leather palm.

I’m wearing a hat, of course, and I find that a ball cap works really well with the hood. You could go in different directions with this, like you could go with like a collared shirt and like a wider-brimmed hat. It’s a little bit of a personal preference.

I’ve always gone with the ball cap because in addition to it fitting well with a hoodie, it also fits well with anything else that you have a hood. So particularly like a rain jacket or a puffy jacket, you can just continue to wear your ball cap.

So we have a pair of sunglasses. This is a critical item, like must-have for anywhere along the Pacific Crest Trail. There’s just lots of sun.

If you’re going up through the High Sierra early as a thru-hiker, you’re also going to be encountering sections that are still snowbound.

If we want to have a really dorky conversation, we could talk about the VLT ratings of your sunglasses. That’s visible light transmission.

If I were going up through the High Sierra early in the season, when there’s still a lot of snow, I actually might even swap out my sunglasses for a pair of glacier goggles for that time of the year. Glacier goggles have like a 5% visible light transmission, whereas a normal like all-purpose pair of sunglasses, you’re looking at maybe like an 8% or 10% lower bound.

You could also go with the photochromic lenses or the transition lenses, which give you a little bit more versatility. You can wear them in mixed light conditions as well as even in the forest because the lens will sort of brighten up for you.

Okay, so for footwear, I’m going to go with a breathable trail-running shoe.

This is the La Sportiva Bushido. It’s my favorite for the Sierra, but I do a lot of like off-trail travel, like hard stuff in the Sierra. This is not probably what I would use for a good A-grade or grade-A trail like the Pacific Crest Trail.

I would be looking at a shoe that has more cushioning, that maybe doesn’t quite have the narrower last of the Bushido. Your classics would be an Altra Lone Peak, maybe a Brooks Cascadia, maybe some of the, what’s that other brand that does the, oh, maybe a pair of Topos.

We might do a future video on how to select footwear for your trip.

I would say generally, if you’re going to be on trail, again, look for something that has some, that it’s comfortable to wear. So it’s cushioned, has a durable outsole because you’re going to be putting a lot of miles on it, and just make sure that it’s very comfortable for you and your natural gait.

Footwear is tough. Footwear is really personalized.

If you find another male who weighs about 160, 165 pounds, I can probably give them the size medium shirt and it will fit them reasonably well and they would be just fine with it.

But if I give them my favorite pair of shoes like this La Sportiva Bushido, even though they might be size 11 and a half, it might not at all work for them.

So shoes are super personal. Make sure to get something that works for you. Don’t just base your decision off of, you know, like some best Pacific Crest Trail backpacking shoes of 2027 video.

Your shoes should be considered a system along with your socks.

What I would recommend doing in the Sierra is that you’re going to have, for most times of the year, it works best to have two pairs of identical socks. So you can call it like hiking pair A and hiking pair B.

And what you’re going to be doing is you’re going to be wearing pair A and then like you’re going to wear them for one full day.

Day two, you put on hiking socks B and you take hiking socks A and you wash them in a creek, no soap, just get that dirt and dust out of the sock just by agitating it in a creek or a lake.

Do consider when you do that, like just that there are other people using the wilderness. So you do it in a place that’s appropriate for having a little bit of your like sock grit back in the water source.

And then once you have your now clean pair of sock A or hiking socks A, you’re going to put these on the back of your backpack and you’re going to let them air-dry on your pack.

I can guarantee you that if you wash them even as late as lunchtime, they will be dry by the end of the day. And then when you get into camp, you can put on your dry, clean sock A and then day four in the morning, you’d wash pair B and you just keep doing the cycle.

So you may have noticed earlier, I do like to wear gaiters. These are the Simblissity LevaGaiters. They remarkably, they sit nicely on the shoe, even without an instep strap.

An instep strap is one of the, it basically goes underneath the shoe and with most trail-running shoes, there’s not an actual instep unlike a boot. So you end up basically stepping on the cord or the strap all the time and that leads to a really short lifespan.

So the Simblissity LevaGaiter, I find that I’ve always worn gaiters. I find that they help keep a lot of stuff out of the shoe. So it prevents things from going in the tops. So particularly like any kind of pebbles, forest debris, like leaves and sticks.

“#TBT to a 70-mile stretch across #JoshuaTreeNationalPark with no natural water sources, part of the #GreatWesternLoop to connect the Grand Canyon with the Pacific Crest Trail.” (Skurka)

Two final items that are part of my go-suit, which again is the category of items I use to describe everything that I’m wearing all the time.

A pair of trekking poles. These are the Black Diamond Alpine Carbon Cork.

You can get lighter poles, but man, the durability of these has just proven to be outstanding. So these poles would, short of user error, these poles will definitely go the distance on the Pacific Crest Trail and they’re also robust enough for any of the high routes.

And then the last item, I do like to wear a watch. This is a very old watch. This is a Suunto Ambit3 Peak. It goes back to 2013.

There are modern GPS watches out there. Any of your Garmins, for example. It’s not necessary to have a GPS watch.

In the Sierra, there are two really useful features of a watch. One is that it just tells time and that’s really helpful to be able to dead reckon as you’re navigating on the Pacific Crest Trail.

The other feature that’s really helpful to have on a watch in the High Sierra is an altimeter.

And if you know your altimeter, then you can play Battleship on your map. So for example, if you’re at 9,800 feet according to your watch and you’re at a trail junction, that will really limit the number of places you can be on your map.

Of course, a lot of you are probably watching this and going like, oh, Andrew’s old. Who still looks at paper maps and plays Battleship with their altimeter? Because everyone nowadays is using FarOut on their phones.

So that’s the go-suit. Now let’s talk about everything that I would keep inside my backpack either all the time or at least some of the time.

This particular pack, this is the Seek Outside Flight. I’ve been using it for multiple seasons and it just, I really like it. It works for me, but there are at least 10, 15 other backpacks out there that have a very similar feature set.

They all weigh in this neighborhood of like two to three pounds. They’re made out of very durable exterior fabric. They have side pockets, like big, nice side pockets, and they also have hip belt pockets. And then finally your mesh or solid-material front pouch.

The ideal volume for a Pacific Crest Trail backpack is going to be in the neighborhood of, I’m going to say 50 liters plus or minus 15.

So if you are like a hardcore thru-hiker, super-ultralighter, maybe you can go down to 35 liters. If you are walking slower and you have quite a few creature comforts and you’re not planning on doing a lot of resupplying during your hike through the High Sierra, maybe you need to be up more towards that 65-liter range.

50, 55 liters, that’s probably the sweet spot for most people.

If you visit the online communities like Reddit Ultralight, you will find lengthy discussions about pack fabrics.

I couldn’t tell you much about modern pack fabrics because the pack fabrics that we had 20 years ago lasted for an entire thru-hike of seven, eight, nine, 11 months. So the modern fabrics are at least as good, probably even better.

I do think it’s worth having a backpack made out of durable materials.

And like even like this mesh pouch, this is the first thing that’s going to get ripped up. And it’s the same thing with the elasticized mesh side pockets. These are the areas that are on the backpack that are actually like vulnerable to the most amount of abrasion.

So I would like this to be like, I’m very happy that these water bottle pockets are made out of the same exterior pack fabric. I wish that this mesh pocket were also made out of it. I think all of these end up being in the neighborhood of like 200-denier-ish.

And this pack and many of the others that fall into this category will last you your Pacific Crest Trail thru-hike, probably, and then some.

Overlooking Roosevelt Lake, on the descent from Don’t Be A Smart Pass

Some pack fabrics are described as waterproof. And I’m specifically thinking of any of the pack fabrics that are laminate with DCF or Dyneema Composite Fabric.

If you have a waterproof pack fabric, that certainly provides a lot of water resistance. I’d be skeptical in not having a more reliable way to waterproof your things, even if you have a pack made out of waterproof fabric.

Those fabrics, especially with the use that a thru-hiker would put on a pack fabric, I wouldn’t count on that pack fabric maintaining its waterproofness long term.

So my solution for waterproofing my things is that I take with me a trash compactor bag. So here it is here. This is made out of two-and-a-half-mil plastic, which is a little bit more, it’s a little bit thicker than like the ultralight pack liners that you’ll see.

The reason I like the pack liners is that they are reliably waterproof. They’re very easy to replace. So you can just drop some in your resupply boxes.

They’re lightweight, and they’re inexpensive. And long term, even after you’ve put thousands of miles on your backpack, they will keep your things dry.

The first one I have closed off about right here. So in that lower pack liner, I have all the things that I am going to need for camp. So my sleeping bag, my sleeping pad, my pillow, my sleeping socks.

And then this upper pack liner would be discretionary. I’m basically going to only use it if it’s pretty evident that I’m going to get rained on.

At that point, before I start getting rained on, I would stop for 10 minutes, pull everything out of my backpack that isn’t protected, line the top of my backpack with my second pack liner, and then seal it up.

Towards the top of my pack, I keep all of my extra clothing. And this extra clothing you can put into two categories.

One category is going to be like environmental protection. So I’m mostly thinking about rain, maybe snow on some other types of trips.

So my rain gear system for the Pacific Crest Trail, it’s going to start with a rain jacket and pants.

It typically does not rain very often or very hard on the Pacific Crest Trail, especially as you get into the peak summer months. So like July, August, September, it doesn’t rain a lot until it does.

Almost all of the rain that you’ll see in the summertime, it’s a monsoonal event. It’s very predictable. You’ll see it in the forecast that there’s some chance of precip.

So maybe it’s a 10% chance of precip. Maybe it’s a 20% chance of precip. Maybe it’s a 40% chance of precip.

And what will happen, you’ll wake up in the morning and there’ll be a bluebird. There’ll be total bluebird sky, not a cloud in the sky. It’s beautiful.

And then by like 10 a.m., you’ll notice that the sky is developing some puffy clouds. And then maybe by like 11, they’re getting like thicker and more and like more of the sky is cloudy.

And then by like noon, you’re starting to get some kind of scary-looking ones, maybe some kind of like violet or like dark blue, maybe some like dark gray.

And then by like one o’clock, you’re starting to see in the distance, you’re starting to see anvil caps on these thunderclouds.

And that’s the sort of day when you actually do need your rain gear.

I have with me a rain jacket and I have with me a pair of rain pants. And I think just because you’re probably not going to see a lot of rain, you can get away typically with some lighter-weight rain gear.

This is the Enlightened Equipment Visp jacket and the matching pants. I think this whole suit together weighs in the neighborhood of maybe like 12 ounces.

If I was going on a shorter trip, so like anything inside of five days, maybe even a week, I would look at the forecast. And if there was no chance of precip on any of those days, I actually would just leave the pants at home. I would leave them in my car.

This would be a last-minute decision. So I would just have a rain jacket. I think it’s poor form to be backpacking without some rain gear.

I also would carry with me some rain mitts.

I personally struggle with, when it rains in the High Sierra or along the Pacific Crest Trail, the temperature also tends to drop a lot.

So I would have a rain mitt system consisting of a liner glove and then a rain mitt. And this would at least give me a fighting chance of keeping my hands functional when the temperatures really drop related to those rainstorms.

Last piece of clothing that I would consider to be part of this environmental protection category is going to be a mid-layer fleece.

Having a mid-layer is really nice to wear for, in two instances. One is if you’re on like a, it’s early in the morning, it’s cold and you want an active layer that provides a little bit of warmth and it feels comfortable to move in.

The other situation it works really well is that you can wear it or layer underneath your rain gear and it will provide you just like a little bit of a buffer between that cold rain on the exterior of your rain jacket and your body.

The other category of clothing that I would take with me would be, I’ll call it like the stop or rest category.

And for the High Sierra, typically I’m just going to bring, I’m going to bring a puffy jacket.

This is the, I don’t remember which model it is. This is made by Katabatic.

It has about three ounces of premium down-fill loft. And for the High Sierra and the Pacific Crest Trail, down fill is totally the way to go.

It gets much better lifespan than synthetic. You can usually keep it dry. And if it does happen to get wet, you can usually get it dry like the next time you get sunshine, which might be later that day. And certainly usually the next day.

Last thing really in this category, I like to bring some headwear insulation. So just, I find a Buff to be pretty versatile.

It’ll keep my ears warm and my head warm.

And then another nice thing about the Buff is that when you get the, if you happen to be out during the full moon, you can put it over your eyes as a sleep mask, and that’s better than waking up in the middle of the night wondering who the hell is putting a flashlight right in your eyes.

The next layer down inside my pack are going to be a lot of food-related items.

So I’m going to take a Ziploc bag, gallon Ziploc bag. And this Ziploc bag is going to have the food that I’m eating today.

I keep this near the top of my pack. I usually put it kind of wrapped up in some of my extra clothing to insulate it.

The hot sun in the High Sierra will absolutely melt anything that could be melted. So especially things like chocolate.

As soon as you enter the High Sierra, you are going to encounter some food storage regulations. And it’s important to know exactly where you are and what those regulations are.

So let me try to break them down for you.

The Sierra High Route (SHR) is a 195-mile trekking route that runs north-south across the heart of the Sierra Nevada Range, through Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, John Muir Wilderness, Ansel Adams Wilderness, and Yosemite National Park. (Skurka)

If you are in Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, so if you’re on the Pacific Crest Trail, you’re going to enter Sequoia-Kings before you reach Mount Whitney.

The regulations are that you need an approved storage method everywhere throughout the park.

An approved storage method means either a hard-sided canister like this one, or they do allow throughout the park, you can, they do allow bear hangs.

So this is the Adotec bear-hanging bag. And then you’ll need a carabiner and maybe 50 feet of cord would be a little thin, maybe 75 feet of cord.

And Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park allows you to hang food, but not everywhere.

So for example, if you are camping at Rae Lakes, you need a hard-sided food canister. If you’re, I believe, Dusy Basin off of Bishop Pass, you’re going to need a hard-sided canister.

As you continue further north, you get into Sierra National Forest or maybe Inyo National Forest. That would be the kind of that, just those jurisdictions to the north. And the regulations there are a little bit more lax.

You could hang your food. You could also use an Ursack, which is a soft stuff sack made out of like a very bite-resistant material. It’s like basically like pure Dyneema.

So those would be options for that section.

Throughout Yosemite National Park, no exceptions, must have a hard-sided bear canister.

If you’re wondering what this bear canister is here, this is the, I think this is called the BV ONE from BearVault.

This is the smaller version. My understanding is that they are coming out with a larger version as well at some point.

And the nice thing about the ONE is that it collapses down. So as your food load, or as you eat through your food, your bear canister will get smaller and smaller and smaller, which is a nice change from your standard BearVaults or Bearikades where it doesn’t matter how much food you have in it. That space is always occupied by the bear canister.

And I have tried, in fact, I’m sure many other people try, you know, you try to put other things in that empty bear canister just to fill up that space.

But for whatever reason, it just seems like whenever you have a bear canister in your backpack, the size of your backpack never gets smaller. It’s like some sort of magic trick, really, just these bear canisters.

A quick note for the 2027 season, you definitely would want to double-check if the ONE is an approved food storage container in Yosemite or in Sequoia-Kings.

It sounds like there may be a moratorium on approving new food storage canisters.

The ONE has been approved by the IGBC, which is the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee. And normally, like Yosemite and Sequoia-Kings, their policies mirror each other.

They accept the same canisters, but they don’t necessarily just accept any canister that’s been IGBC-approved.

A good case in point is that the Ursack, for example, has been approved by the IGBC, but it is not accepted. It’s not an acceptable food storage method in Yosemite or in Sequoia-Kings.

Okay, so the last item related to food is going to be my stove.

I still prefer an alcohol stove for the High Sierra, and I would take one on the Pacific Crest Trail. I’m going to give you some caveats, though.

First is that the denatured alcohol is now difficult to find in California.

You still can, though, find if you go into a gas station, you’ll often find the bottle of, it’s ideally the yellow bottle of HEET, H-E-E-T, which is used as a gas-line antifreeze.

You could also use the red bottle. My understanding is that might be a little bit more toxic, but I don’t think it probably makes a huge difference if you’re in a well-ventilated space.

The reason I like the alcohol stoves are they’re quiet. I can carry just the right amount of fuel instead of being in that, like, do I need a four-ounce can? Do I need an eight-ounce can? Is a partially used eight-ounce can, is this going to be enough to get me to my next resupply?

And then when, on very short trips, the alcohol stove system is also lighter because you just don’t have that overhead weight of that canister, of like that metal canister, and the stove unit itself is also lighter.

This is the Kojin stove from Trail Designs. This weighs less than any canister stove, like an MSR PocketRocket, that you’ll find out there.

I totally get why a lot of thru-hikers and Pacific Crest Trail hikers would want to just go with a canister stove.

Those canisters are going to be available at most of the resupply points in any of the hostels. You’re going to find them in the hiker boxes.

I think I’m just sort of wedded for a long time to my alcohol stove, and I’m reluctant to give it up.

The other caveat I would add to the alcohol stove system is that there is a responsible-use issue here.

When you light this fuel during the daytime, it’s very difficult to actually see the flame.

So if you ever, for example, run out of fuel, like your stove goes out of fuel before your meal is cooked, don’t just pour more fuel in there.

What you want to do is put your hand slowly over the stove and make sure that it’s completely out.

I’ve done this before, where you pour and you accidentally light your fuel bottle on fire. It can be a real danger.

The other danger with the alcohol stoves is that you have this measuring cup and you can pour your fuel into the measuring cup, and then if you just pour it into your stove, inevitably like a drop or two of the fuel is going to end up somewhere around the stove and not in the stove itself.

So the best practice is that you measure out your fuel and then pour the fuel into your stove somewhere else besides where you’re going to cook.

And then at that point I would go ahead and light my stove and I put on top.

The danger is that if you pour some fuel around here by accident, light it, you’re going to light the ground on fire.

So you can easily end up with a ground fire or a forest debris fire if you’re not careful.

To eat, I prefer a spoon with a big ladle on it and a shortened handle.

This fits nicely into my ditty kit. And I prefer a plastic spoon over a metal spoon. It’s less sharp on the teeth.

It’s not cold to the touch. It doesn’t have like the nails-on-a-chalkboard sound when I’m eating out of my pot, which is my preference.

And then to light my stove, I prefer just a little Mini Bic lighter.

I usually carry, not I usually, I always carry two lighters with me.

I keep one in my ditty kit and I keep another in another part of my backpack. And by having two lighters, I make sure that if one gets wet, I always have a backup.

Do not make the mistake of putting your lighter inside your pot. And this would apply for alcohol stoves and for canister stoves.

There’s enough, typically after a meal, there’s enough residual moisture inside of a pot that you can get your lighter wet enough that you’re going to struggle to start it.

So keep it in a dry place that’s not inside your pot.

I can’t forget these two items. This is part of my food kit as well.

This is a very inexpensive plastic cutting board that I chopped into a circle and it fits nicely inside of a bear canister.

I like to make kind of a more legitimate lunch. So typically say like cheese, salami, and crackers.

I also like to carry with me a real knife. So this is the Opinel, I think this is the No. 6, super-sharp knife and a very basic, very lightweight.

And it’s nice to have a real knife when you’re cutting real food like cheese or salami or butter.

“My stove system for solo backpacking trips in the shoulder seasons, when I’m willing to carry a few extra ounces so that I can quickly heat up large amounts of water. With a larger pot and an additional eating container, mug, and utensil, this system would be suitable for couples, too.” (Skurka)

This is the pack liner from the bottom of my backpack. Let’s take a look at what’s in it.

Again, these are going to be items that I do not need during the day. They are explicitly only for camp.

Let’s start by talking about the shelter.

For all of the High Sierra trips that I’ve been doing recently, I’ve been using the Mid from HMG.

It weighs 20 ounces. It’s very storm-resistant. It’s bug-proof. It has a waterproof floor.

It’s a shelter that I can start using at the beginning of the backpacking season in June. And I can use it all the way through the end of the season at the end of September, beginning of October, even at times of the year where it’s overkill.

So for example, August, beginning of September, where the temperatures are still very mild and there are no bugs. So technically I don’t need bug protection.

And the forest floor is also pretty dry by that time of the year. So I don’t need a super-robust groundsheet.

It’s overkill for those conditions, but like, man, it’s only 20 ounces. So it’s just a shelter that works really well.

If you’re a thru-hiker, this is the sort of shelter that you could use from start to finish.

The other shelters in this category would be something like the Zpacks Duplex, which is a two-person version. They also have the Soloplex, the Altaplex.

With shelters like the HMG Mid and this larger category of shelters that rely on trekking poles to be pitched, all of these shelters are only as good as your weakest stake because they require tension to stay pitched.

Personally, I take with me about eight stakes. These are the Easton nails. I think they’re seven inches long.

They weigh about two-thirds of an ounce. And I know that there are lighter-weight stakes out there. You can find them made out of carbon fiber. You can find titanium skewers.

But I just think for, you’re not talking about a lot of extra weight.

And the peace of mind that I get from stakes that aren’t going to pull out of the ground, and then I can pound into compacted ground with a granite rock, is well worth it to me.

An assortment of single- and double-wall tents on the Alaskan tundra. (Skurka)

For my sleeping bag, last season I moved over to the Western Mountaineering SummerLite, which is a true mummy bag with a real hood.

So yeah, you heard it here first. I no longer use quilts.

When I first started backpacking 20, 25 years ago, quilts were a dramatic improvement over what was available at the time, just in terms of the warmth per weight.

But the traditional sleeping bag companies like Western caught up. They started using similarly lightweight shell fabrics. They also use the same super-high-quality down.

So I have found that just the quilts, they’re drafty. That’s what it comes down to.

And as I got older, I just was struggling like every time I kind of rolled over, you know, doing the nightly rotisserie action.

I just got sick and tired of that draft. So last season, I upgraded to a mummy bag.

It’s been fantastic. It’s rated to 32 degrees, which is a pretty conservative rating. It weighs 19 ounces.

If I were starting the Pacific Crest Trail from Mexico, I think a 32-degree bag, that feels about right to me.

I know you’re in the desert for the first 700 miles, but you’re there in, you’re there in May or in April or maybe even March.

It’s not, it’s not particularly warm at that time of the year, especially at night. So I think having a bag that you can take below freezing, it would be, would give you some comfort. It would make sure that you’re sleeping well every night.

I think as you go further north, if you were going to use a bag, I think it would actually be north of the High Sierra.

You know, when you’re in like Northern California, when you’re in Oregon during like late July, August, during those like dog days of those hot days of summer.

I think at that point, maybe you could go with a lightweight bag that was more of a comfort rating, say like 40 degrees.

There’s an argument for just having a kit that is versatile, versatile enough to make it pretty much the entire trip where those like two or three ounces don’t warrant the hassle of sending stuff home and getting stuff in the mail or the extra expense of $400, $500, $600 for an entirely different sleep system.

So the deal with the comfort ratings, you know, this has improved a lot with the standard that they have now. Because you can get a little bit more apples-to-apples, but none of the quilts are rated according to that standard.

You tend to sleep warmer if you have a, if you’re like thicker-bodied and if you’re young and if you have a lot of muscle.

For a sleeping pad, back when I was young, I used to just go with closed-cell foam, but nowadays I have, like so many other people, upgraded to the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite.

This for, boy, probably 15, maybe even 20 years now has been the gold standard for warmth to weight and comfort.

There are other pads out there that are warmer. There are pads out there that are lighter. There are pads out there that are more comfortable.

I’m not sure any of them have figured out how to get that exact, like this, this perfect intersection of comfort and warmth and weight.

If you’re young and you don’t have a lot of money, a closed-cell foam pad is fine.

It’s not as comfortable, but you’re young and they’re not going to deflate on you.

I do think that the air pads, they’re durable-ish, but boy, you’re asking a lot of an 11-ounce product that holds air every single night to make it through the length of a thru-hike.

So I would at least know that maybe my, the pad that I start with is not going to be the pad that I finish with.

And I would also make sure if I were on a thru-hike carrying a NeoAir XLite or similar, that I would have a patch kit and I would know how to use it.

And I would know how to find holes in my pad, particularly the slow leakers that get annoying night after night after night when you’re having to wake up two or three times to reinflate your pad.

In addition to the sleeping pad, I also carry with me a pillow.

This is a little two-and-a-half-ounce luxury. Maybe this is a three-ounce luxury.

This is one that I’ve used from Sea to Summit.

It’s pretty old at this point, but it’s kind of the right size and it’s the right, it’s like a nice comfortable fabric on top.

There are definitely lighter pillows. There are bigger pillows, but this one works pretty well for me.

To finish up, let’s talk about some of the things that are on the outside of my pack.

These are items that I’m, that I intentionally keep on the outside because I want them accessible.

In my side pockets, I have, I just carry a one-liter, that’ll go in the Smartwater bottle.

Nowadays, instead of ingesting these microplastics, you can go with the commercial bottles that look like a Smartwater bottle. I’m thinking like the ones from CNOC.

In my back mesh pocket, I have with me a coffee cup.

I do like carrying a coffee cup. I find that my breakfasts are more efficient if I have one, because I can make hot water for both breakfast and coffee at the same time.

I have a Platy bottle. This is a two-and-a-half-liter Platy bottle. There are other options out there.

Water is abundant in the High Sierra. If you’ve been, if you have come through Southern California, you’ll never have an issue with water.

If you are in the desert, maybe you want two of these because for some of those longer stretches, maybe even three of these, if you’re hiking late in the year and the water sources aren’t very reliable.

These are great for carrying large amounts of water. They don’t weigh a whole lot.

You’re going to want at least one of these, even in areas where water is abundant, because it allows you to fill up all of your capacity at the very end of the day, and then hike another hundred yards, 200 yards, 400 yards to your campsite.

And you’re not having to go back and forth to go get water for breakfast or for dinner.

I carry it with me. I like to carry a sunglass case. I leave it in the outside pouch.

The sunglasses, as we talked about before, they’re a critical item for the Pacific Crest Trail. You’re going to be wearing them all the time.

You have something that’s going to protect your sunglasses. If your sunglasses were to go down, it’s going to be a pretty uncomfortable couple of days before you can get some replacements.

In my other side pocket, so if you’re a Pacific Crest Trail hiker, you’re not going to be carrying paper maps. You’re just going to be looking at your phone, following the FarOut app.

But if you are doing any of the other itineraries that are available to you in the Sierra, so suppose you’re doing a high route or you’re doing some kind of DIY itinerary, and still for all of my trips, I love to carry paper maps.

I find that, especially when you’re navigating off-trail, having your maps, it’s a custom map set printed out on 11-by-17 paper.

This just provides so much more topographical context about what I’m seeing versus looking at my phone with the six-inch screen.

The other nice thing about paper maps is that the contour interval never changes.

So unlike pinching and zooming, it can be a little difficult to do that terrain association where you’re trying to get your mind to start understanding how the proximity of contour lines on the map relate to the field and vice versa.

Dynamic contour lines, it can be difficult because that relationship is constantly changing.

But here on the map, it’s printed. I can very easily kind of tell what’s going on.

And then I also like to carry with me a magnetic compass.

I just have this compass girth-hitched to my shoulder strap.

For the Pacific Crest Trail thru-hiker, you’re not going to need a magnetic compass.

But for anyone who’s a little bit more old-school, it’s a nice thing to have in the High Sierra just to get your bearings, kind of understand where is north, and maybe occasionally take some bearings in places where you’re not on a trail or maybe where the snow is covering your trail.

“Navigating around Alaska, the old-fashioned way, with an 11″x17″ USGS map (created with National Geographic TOPO! software) and a simple baseplate compass (located in my side pocket, attached via the lanyard to my shoulder strap).” (Skurka)

Okay, and last but not least, I have my hip belt pockets in here.

I carry my water purification. I like to use Aquamira, and I bring with me a premix bottle.

The big problem with the Aquamira, we’ve used it in our guiding program for many years. It has an awesome track record.

It can purify large amounts of water very quickly, which is a great thing in a group setting or if you’re backpacking in the, where you might leave a water source with, you know, seven, eight, nine liters of water, and that’s a lot of water to send through a Sawyer Squeeze.

So the Aquamira will purify that water much more quickly than a manual filter.

The big problem with it, though, is that you have two shelf-stable solutions, part A, part B, and the recommended system is that you do seven drops of A and seven drops of B, and you let it sit in this mixing cap for five minutes, and then you can put that in your water, and that’s sort of a nuisance.

So what we do is we bring these premix bottles.

This is a 10-milliliter bottle, and what I can do with this bottle is I can do, in a group, I can actually do 80 drops of A and 80 drops of B, and this premix will be good for probably two, maybe even three days.

We try to use it up in 24 hours just to be careful.

It actually doesn’t reach its maximum potency until after about 90 minutes, so you’ve got like a super, super potent premix in here if you wait 90 minutes.

Okay, last thing in here. Here we go. Just some personal hygiene and skin items.

I carry with me some sunscreen. I do like to have a dedicated lip balm, ideally with some sunscreen in it.

And then the last thing I have with me, this is a mini dropper bottle with Dr. Bronner’s soap.

I’m a big advocate of the backcountry bidet, so I don’t need to use any toilet paper at all, and the hand soap is the way to clean up and make sure that I’m not getting myself sick or anyone else in my group.

Yeah, we have an entire video, in fact the first video that we ever did with The Trek, dedicated to the backcountry bidet.

Go ahead and make sure to watch that. Maybe you’ll be a convert too.

In fact, I would actually, if you are a Pacific Crest Trail hiker, I would strongly encourage you to just move to the backcountry bidet.

With all of the use on the Pacific Crest Trail, toilet paper is a major problem, especially down in those desert sections where there just isn’t enough organic soil to break down the toilet paper.

So do your part in just converting to the backcountry bidet and not leaving a trace at all those high-impact campsites down there in SoCal.

Last but not least, I have a couple of little ditty items.

So this is the one that has items I don’t need very often.

So I have my battery charger. You’re going to need 10,000 milliamp-hours, maybe 20,000 milliamp-hours, as well as your charging cables.

This is the Nitecore, I think it’s the NU27.

It’s light, it’s got a red light on it, it has a lockout, it’s bright enough to hike at night, although I don’t really like to hike at night.

I have with me a little bit of Dawn dish soap.

This is really nice for cleaning my sunglasses. I’m wearing my sunglasses all the time. They get covered in dust, they get covered in grease from my fingers, so having the ability to clean your sunglasses is really nice.

And the last thing I keep in that bag, this is my satellite messenger.

You could go with the Garmin inReach, and I would totally understand that.

I’ve been using the ZOLEO for a long time.

The big draw for me with the ZOLEO is that they give me a dedicated phone number, so if anyone needs to get hold of me, they can just text just like they would anyone else, as opposed to Garmin’s mind-blowingly complex obsolete system of needing to log into a MapShare page and sending someone a message through this MapShare page.

And then once that communication is established, then it’s a little bit more normal texting.

In my other ditty bag, these are mostly just little toiletry items.

I have with me another lighter. I have with me, this is GurneyGoo, which is for foot care, mostly for preventing skin maceration of my feet.

A little toothbrush. And then for toothpaste, I actually just use Dr. Bronner’s.

It’s an acquired taste, but it allows me to not have to bring toothpaste.

And the Dr. Bronner’s, a lot less of it is needed, probably like three drops minimum. And if you go with five drops, you’re like foaming at the mouth.

I bring some earplugs with me in case I’m sharing my campsite with some snorers.

I have some floss picks because I kind of get weirded out by putting my fingers in my mouth on backpacking trips.

And a bite guard because I’m one of those people. Surprise, surprise.

And then a little, this is just a pill case or pill bag with mostly just ibuprofen for pain reliever and a headache reducer.

I have some Tylenol in there and some Benadryl to help me sleep occasionally, or if I have some sort of allergic reaction.

I would also carry on a personal trip, I’d be carrying some antidiarrheal.

The one thing I don’t have in here, just because I didn’t bring it today, I would absolutely be carrying a little personal stock of Leukotape.

There’s another video we did about my entire first aid kit and also about foot care.

So definitely would be carrying some Leukotape in there.

There’s a huge gap to go from day hiking to backpacking. You just need so much more gear for backpacking.

So I know it’s a lot, but hopefully it was helpful.

There’s some things that I’m not taking on the Pacific Crest Trail.

I’m not taking sleeping clothes because I’m not expecting to get rained on very often and probably not very heavily.

And I just don’t think it’s worth that like three-quarters of a pound to either sleep, to make sure that every night I’m sleeping dry.

Every day you should be washing your socks. Every day you should be trying to wash your feet.

Every other day you should be trying to do like a crotch-and-pits wash.

Your hiking shirt should get washed every like three days, four days at the most. It kind of depends on what kind of sweater you are.

Underwear is like for males every other day, maybe every third day. For women I think it’s more like socks where it should be like a daily wash.

I did in the video talk about just like the extra context and regulations around food storage.

That’s an important thing with this. Like the agencies, they try really hard to keep human-bear conflicts to a minimum and maybe prevent them outright.

The Park Service and the National Forest lands, the Forest Service have made huge strides in the last 20 years in that.

When you talk to old-school backpackers or old-timers from the High Sierra, they have just epic stories of crazy things that bears did to get human food.

And nowadays you really don’t have those sorts of stories anymore.

There are some items that I would describe as being like conditions-dependent.

So rain pants and rain mitts. If I were on a thru-hike, I would just have it packed because I think you’re out there long enough that you’re going to see heavy enough rain that you do want rain pants, you do want rain mitts.

But if you’re doing more of like a shorter section hike, say like five days, maybe seven days, it’s something that you could leave behind.

The puffy jacket and the mid-layer in the summertime, so like July, maybe August, that could be an either-or item.

You might not need both, so it’d be a little bit weather-dependent.

There are times of the year, especially like later in the summer, where you could get away with a lighter shelter.

It’s probably not going to rain on you and you’re not having bug pressure anymore.

So that might be the time of year where you just carry like a very small flat tarp or maybe an A-frame tarp.

Maybe go with a tarp and bivy. Maybe you just go with a tarp and groundsheet.

If you are a female, you’re going to, you will want to carry one extra pair of underwear.

Males, you can just carry one and you’re just washing and air-drying them. Or not air-drying, you’re actually wear-drying them, where you wash your underwear, you put your underwear back on, and you keep on hiking and it will dry out for you.

But for women, two pairs would be appropriate.

And then women also make sure to just add some items for your hair and menstrual products.

And then finally, I didn’t at all talk about early-season conditions.

So if you are a thru-hiker, you’re going to be going up through the High Sierra early in the season.

You might be there in May. You’re going to be there in the beginning of June.

If you’re like totally crazy, you might be there in April.

You’re going to need glacier glasses. You’re going to need an ice axe.

You’re going to need something like a sit pad. And you’d also want some puffy pants.

At that time of the year where it’s not backpacking, it’s almost a little bit more like mountaineering.

And if you catch it early enough, you’re kind of wondering where your skis are.

So I would recommend that you prepare accordingly, not just with what you’re carrying, but also just be prepared for those conditions.

“Walking on concrete-hard snow below Muir Pass in mid-May, early in the morning. A few hours later in this same spot, I would have been postholing up to my waist.” (Skurka)

With the bear canister, I would bet that my base weight, as I just kind of showed you, would be in like low teens.

You pull out that bear canister and you’re closer to 10.

And I’m certain that if a couple of you are watching this video and you’re like, what? 10? I can get it down to six.

And there certainly is the gear and the information out there to do that nowadays.

I think the reason that I’ve chosen the gear that I have is I want a kit that I can use for almost the entire hiking season and not have to swap things in and out a lot.

And the other thing I would say is that I’ve done that six-pound base weight thing.

And it’s really nice for hiking, but your margins are pretty thin.

I just don’t really have the tolerance at the age of 45 to be suffering that much. And often as a trip leader to be running things that thinly.

So by all means, if you can get it down to five or six pounds, all the more power to you.

But I think a lot of people are going to be more comfortable bumping it up a little bit.

It’s not that much extra weight. And that extra weight goes a long way in terms of your comfort and your margins.

If you live in the Denver metro area, we’d love you to join that live podcast. It’s going to be at Skylark Lounge, Saturday, December 5th. You can get tickets using the link down in the description.

We are opening registration for my guided trips on Monday, December 7th, if you’re interested in joining us in one of our locations.

And I’ll see you next week, Monday at noon Mountain Time for the next episode.

#8446. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8444. ATN Thor 6 First Look: The One and Done Thermal Scope?

Published Oct 26, 2026 5:56 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

There is a dizzying array of thermal scopes on the market, and finding the right one for you typically starts with deciding how you’ll use it. Are you hunting hogs over bait? Or calling in predators in open country?

Those two use cases are on either end of the thermal scope spectrum. You really don’t need to spend $10,000 on a scope with a 1280 sensor for close-range hog hunting. A 640 or even 384 optic with a lower base magnification is plenty for that job. On the other hand, David Stroud, a serious competition predator hunter, once told me, “The best is barely good enough,” for his use case.

But, after testing the ATN Thor 6 -LRF, I found it’s a scope that can do just about anything. It’s not completely overgunned — or overpriced — for hog hunting, and the 640 variant is plenty capable for predator hunting. The added LRF, ballistic calculator, and easy controls make it a solid all-around optic. Here’s what I think of it after initial testing and a detailed comparison of the 13 different Thor 6 models.

The Thor 6 LRF has a 1,000-meter rangefinder built into the scope. There’s a dedicated ranging button that’s easy to find in the dark. If you have the ballistic calculator set up, the adjusted aiming point will automatically appear. This system makes shooting at night much easier because you have zero depth perception through a night optic.

The Thor 6 has the form factor of a traditional scope, which makes it easier to use in the pitch dark. Instead of a series of buttons, you have a combination of knobs and buttons for your critical adjustments. The focus control is where you’ll typically find the parallax knob on a traditional scope. You’ll navigate the menu using the elevation turret. The zoom and ocular focus controls are in the same spot as a standard scope. The buttons to start recording video and range targets are large and easy to reach.

One of the hardest parts of getting a thermal scope into the field is figuring out the menus, zeroing it, and just figuring out how the thing works. I’ve tested dozens of thermals and I still get tripped up by some optics. ATN saves you from thumbing through the owner’s manual and watching YouTube tutorials to figure out your new scope. There’s a built-in AI assistant within the ATN app. You can ask it any questions you have, and it will give you the answers. The app is also where you can review your video recordings, stream a live view, and adjust settings.

Thermal scopes are expensive and they have delicate sensors that can be damaged by sunlight. One of the easiest ways to damage your scope is to leave the objective lens uncovered in direct sunlight. ATN helps you mitigate that by outfitting the scope with a lens cap that’s actually quite good and a neoprene cover. They’re nice accessories to have straight out of the box.

Much is made of a thermal scope’s resolution and image quality. But, I think the big differentiator is the user experience. I want a scope that’s easy to zero, easy to adjust, and that I can use while blindfolded. Fumbling around in the dark for the focus or burning a box of ammo to get zeroed are the experiences I avoid like a coyote with mange.

So I was relieved that the ATN Thor 6 was easy to mount and get zeroed. I set one of the included thermal targets at 50 yards and opened up the zeroing setting. Then I fired a shot and checked its location with a spotting scope. Next, I adjusted the zero by moving the reticle from my aim point to the impact location. It’s a simple process, and you can even freeze the image to make it more precise. My next shot was within a few inches of my aim point, and after a small adjustment, I was dead on with my third shot. I moved the target to 100 yards to get my final zero, which required only two shots. So with five shots, I had the scope zeroed and the chronograph data I needed to set up the ballistic calculator.

After zeroing and setting up the ballistic calculator, I started shooting targets at various ranges. The ballistic calculator worked as I expected, with first round impacts at all distances. I’ve had some scopes that refresh constantly and seriously disrupt your ability to scan for animals. The Thor 6 has long a period between refreshes, which I appreciated. After shooting this scope on the range, I can’t say enough good things about how easy the menu is to navigate and how intuitive the controls are.

I’ve spent the last few years falling down the thermal optics rabbit hole, doing everything from an annual trip to Texas to test the latest in night optics to managing predators on my lease. While I’ve tested a ton of different optics, the one constant has been a Horizon Firearms rifle in .22 Creedmoor. The Horizon rifles are unquestionably accurate, handy, light, and the best turnkey coyote gun I’ve used. My current rifle is a Vandal 2 with an 18-inch barrel and chambered in .22 Creed. It shoots 80-grain Hornady ELD Match at 3,018 fps and easily maintains sub-MOA accuracy. The bare rifle weighs around 7 pounds, which is light enough to be handy but still heavy enough for stability. On the muzzle end, I added a Dead Air Nomad Ti OTB, which is an over-the-barrel suppressor. Its design keeps the gun short because only half the suppressor extends beyond the muzzle. The ATN Thor 6 rounds out the build nicely because it’s a truly versatile optic.

#8441. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8440. Dreaded Message Received — John Muir Trail Day 4

After summiting Mount Whitney I went to sleep early, and for the first stretch I slept soundly and deeply.  So soundly, in fact, that when I woke my bladder was already near bursting and I had to run out to find a tree to pee against.  Sometimes when it is cold, or raining, you are tempted to wait a while longer to venture out.  Not this time!

Later during the night I left the tent three more times with a full bladder.  Maybe it was a response to the day at altitude?  Unfortunately, the good deep sleep came only during the first stretch.  After that it was interrupted with incessant severe coughing and blowing my nose.  I kept hoping to get over this thing and it kept hanging on.

I got up fairly late in the morning; it was already after seven o’clock.  This did not worry me as we had a relatively short day planned.  I went to the stream to rinse out my shorts and to wash my sock liners.  I pack two pairs of liners to use on alternate days, and I try to wash the “dirty” pair each day while I wear the other one.  Of course, washing in cold water with no soap does not work perfectly, but it helps.

On my way back from the creek, Sam accosted me.  “George, we gotta play some frisbee.”

I agreed and we started tossing it back-and-forth.  Once again, I was not delivering very good passes, but what started to worry me more was my breath.   I was not running downfield routes for the disc; we were just standing there calmly throwing back-and-forth.  Yet after maybe 15-20 throws I realized I was getting out of breath.  Really sucking air, but why?  Sure, we were camped at over 10,000 feet elevation, but that should not have been affecting me so much by Day Four.  I quit and went to get my Garmin.

My Garmin inReach looks huge, but it is barely longer than my middle finger

The Garmin InReach is a handy communications device in the wilderness.  For an emergency, it has an SOS function designed to bring the search-and-rescue folks running.  For everyday use, it allows text communication by satellite where there is no phone signal.  That is the case on much of the John Muir Trail.  Just be prepared to spend some real time painstakingly typing in one letter at a time!  What is more, under heavy overcast skies the satellite connection is limited, and that had prevented me from notifying my wife the night before that we had summited Mt. Whitney.

Now in the morning I sent out the word, and I got a dreaded message in reply.

Let me go back a year.  In 2025, during my hike of the Long Trail in Vermont, my son Ben developed an appendicitis that turned out to be colon cancer.  I wrote about this in last year’s blog on The Trek.  After surgery, he went through a dozen rounds of chemotherapy, after which a scan showed him to be cancer free.  In celebration he and his wife went to Greece and my wife Lee and I went to Vermont to take care of our granddaughters while they were gone.  Just a few weeks after our return, and before I headed to the John Muir Trail, they found some nodules on his follow-up scan.  They said these might just be scar tissue from his surgery and we ardently hoped they were only that.

But I was skeptical.  Why would this scar tissue, from a year-old surgery, not have shown up on the earlier scan, but only showed up now?  The plan was to have another scan in 4-6 weeks to see what it looked like.  That would have come close to the end of my John Muir Trail hike (if I were successful).  However, Ben’s blood markers were highly concerning and, unbeknownst to me, they moved up his scan date.  Now my wife sent me the bad news through the Garmin.  The scan showed that the cancer had returned with a vengeance.  Ben now had Stage Four colon cancer.  It felt like a gut punch to me; no doubt worse for him.

Moments later, Lee texted me again.  She was going to the Emergency Room with our friend and neighbor Susan.  She didn’t say why or even whether she was taking Susan for treatment or Susan was taking her.  Shortly before leaving on the trail Lee had her appendix out.  When it was getting time for me to leave, she assured me that she was much, much better and she urged me to go.  Apparently, that was not entirely true, and she was in a lot of pain in her incision.  It was made worse by her coughing, as it seems I had generously shared my own illness with her before I left.

I texted her asking whether I should leave the trail and she replied, “No, not yet.”  I was not sure whether she realized that my offer to leave the trail – given where I was located – was intended for several days in the future.  A swift departure from where I stood then would have required a helicopter.  I decided not to clarify that, although – with my breathing difficulties – I wondered whether I might actually need the chopper myself before long.

Yes, it was an awful morning between my son’s cancer, my wife in the Emergency Room, and my own health issues.  I was tempted to return to my tent and launch headfirst back into my sleeping bag and not come out.  Instead, I made breakfast, used the campsite’s well-designed three-sided privy, and packed up.

As we set off, we followed the same route as we had in the dark the night before.  First, over the stream on a pair of logs and then up a couple of small slopes to the John Muir Trail.  This time, when we got there, we would turn left, northbound, instead of right toward Mount Whitney.

The two small slopes were nothing really.  But they left me gasping and wheezing.  The same person who had ascended over 4,000 feet just the day before was now struggling with less than 100 feet.  I truly worried how I would make it through the day.

I was thinking I needed to get off trail with Sam at Onion Valley, but that felt impossibly distant.  Could I make it over Forrester Pass?  Could I even make it to our intended campsite tonight at Tyndall Creek?

Luckily the first part of the trail was gently sloped.  What I gradually discovered was that if it was level or downhill I could handle it pretty well.  The uphills by contrast were killing me, having to catch my breath gasping for air, and dealing with this perpetual cough and blowing my nose.  This is disgusting, I know, but I realized that my handkerchief could not hold all the mucus I was producing.  So, after blowing my nose, I found a stone or stick to wipe it out of my filthy rag and to fling it away from the trail.

As we continued with the mild gradient, I started feeling a bit stronger.  That was certainly a relief.  Some of the trees by the trail had amazing textures as well, and the scenery around me distracted me.

Amazing close-up showing the texture of some exposed tree-trunk.

The improvement continued until I felt almost normal  when we stopped  for a midday snack at a river crossing and filled our water containers.  At that point the weather was ominous with a lot of big thunderheads rumbling and rain threatening.  I regretted that our late start might have pushed us into the bad weather window.   We were both anticipating having to wear our rain gear.  At that river crossing I took my rain poncho out of my backpack and put it in my front left pocket.  It was bulky and a little annoying there, but it was the best I could do to have it accessible if or when the skies opened up.

Stark bare tree reaching into the sky (and note the thunderclouds behind it!)

The bulky pocket turned out to be a good rain prevention device, because the rest of the day we only got brief sprinkles despite the ominous clouds all around.  Beyond the creek the path turned uphill in a way that would have crushed me that morning.  Now my stronger legs propelled me upward, slowly but without breaking my spirit.  The beautiful countryside inspired me as well.  Eventually we emerged from the forest into an area of open views called the Bighorn Plateau.  There we could see the mountains encircling us and in the grasses were ravens foraging for I-know-not-what.

From the plateau the trail went downhill to our planned campsite at Tyndall Creek.  Our intention was to camp on the far north side of the cluster of tent sites scattered along the creek to be closer to Forrester Pass the next morning.  But folks already camped told us the far side was crowded and possibly already filled.

Therefore, we took  the first pleasant spot with two tent sites available and made our camp.  Nearby we met another camper named Daniel.  He was a friendly fellow and we chatted.  He told us he was a 35-year-old pharmacist living in Portland.  His father Norm, and his father’s friend Brian, were hiking SOBO and would be meeting up with him if they could get over Forrester Pass the next day.  He told us that Brian was Chinese and nursing a knee injury, so that we might identify the two older hikers if we encountered them the next day.  We could tell them that Daniel was waiting for them.

After a nice dinner with Brian, I recited Edgar Allen Poe’s poem “The Raven” which confirmed just how much my breath had improved over the course of the day.  Sam actually filmed me doing it and, other than one coughing fit and one memory lapse, I gave a respectable performance.

Then it was time for the nightly ablutions.  I even dug my cathole to be ready after breakfast in the morning.  At 8:30 p.m. I set my alarm for 4:30 a.m., giving me exactly eight hours of sleep if I could manage it.

In my tent, nestled in my sleeping bag, I thought of Ben and his battle with cancer, and Lee dealing with that and with her own health issues.   While on the trail there is too much focus on the right here and right now, one step in front of the other, to think much of those things.  But once settled down they seep back into consciousness.  The stormy overcast of the day had matched my mood, and I felt sorrowful as I dozed off.

Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years.
